sentences.text: In late winter and early spring, sap rises inside sugar maple trees.
Sap is the tree's watery juice. It is mostly water, with a little sugar mixed in.
On warm days after freezing nights, the sap can drip from a small tap in the trunk.
People collect the drips in buckets or in tubes that run downhill to a tank.
The sap does not taste like syrup yet. It is thin and only gently sweet.
In a sugarhouse, the sap is boiled in wide, shallow pans.
Water turns to steam and floats away, and the sugar stays behind.
As the liquid gets thicker, it becomes maple syrup.
It takes about 40 gallons of sap to make about 1 gallon of syrup.
That is why the boiling takes a long time and why syrup is more precious than the fresh sap.
The color can be golden or deep amber, depending on when the sap was collected.
Real maple syrup comes from this tree sap, not from stirring sugar into water at the table.

questions.prompt: What is this passage mostly about?

choices.text: How maple sap is collected and boiled into syrup
How to paint a tree golden or amber
Why buckets are made of sugar
How winter nights freeze a whole river

questions.explanation: The passage starts with sap rising in maple trees and ends with thick syrup after boiling. The whole process is the main idea.

questions.prompt: About how much sap makes one gallon of syrup?
questions.explanation: The passage gives the comparison directly: about 40 gallons of sap make about 1 gallon of syrup.

questions.prompt: In this passage, sap is what?

choices.text: A metal tap with no use
Sugar stirred in at the table

questions.explanation: The passage says sap is the tree's watery juice, mostly water with a little sugar. That is the meaning to use.

questions.prompt: Why does boiling make the sap taste stronger and thicker?

choices.text: The pans add forty new kinds of sugar
Freezing nights stir the pans by themselves
The color amber is mixed in with a spoon
Water leaves as steam, so the sugar that stays is more concentrated

questions.explanation: The passage says water turns to steam and the sugar stays. From that clue, a reader can figure out that what remains is thicker and more strongly sweet.
